title: Woe that day
hook: the refrain repeated ten times: woe that day to the deniers (77:15)

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-mursalat, and your line: sent forth. What kept arriving for you, wind, breath, a sound? Today, the second half of al-Mursalat, and the last day of this stretch of the book. Day six hundred sixty-three.

Some songs are built on a chorus. The verse changes, the story moves, and then the same line comes back, and by the third time the listener is waiting for it. Earlier this year, ar-Rahman did that with a question, which of your Lord's favors will you deny, again and again. Al-Mursalat does it too, with a shorter line and a heavier one. It comes back ten times in fifty verses, and the whole surah is built around it.

Surah seventy-seven, verse fifteen, in Pickthall's translation: "Woe unto the repudiators on that day!" In Arabic, waylun yawma'idhin lil-mukadhdhibin. Wayl is woe, a cry of ruin. Yawma'idhin, on that day, the Day the surah has been describing. And al-mukadhdhibin comes from the root k-dh-b, to lie. The form here means more than people who doubt. It's people who call a true thing a lie, who look at it and say, that's false. Pickthall's old word, repudiators, catches that: people who disown what's in front of them. Now watch where the refrain falls. It doesn't only follow scenes of the end. Again and again it follows a gift. Did We not create you from a humble fluid, and shape you? Woe that day to the deniers. Did We not make the earth a place that holds the living and the dead, and set firm mountains on it, and give you sweet water to drink? Woe that day to the deniers. The warning keeps landing right after something good. Some commentators read it that way: the denial in view isn't only of the Day, but of the gifts that point to it. To be handed water, a body, solid ground, and call the giver a fiction. So the refrain works in two directions. It's a warning about the end. And it's a nudge about this afternoon: what good thing in front of you have you been quietly treating as nothing?

The practice: deny nothing good today. Sit, and take an honest inventory of the last day. Look for one good thing you brushed off. A compliment you waved away. A meal someone made that you ate standing up. A message you meant to answer. A morning you woke up healthy and didn't notice. Hold it for a moment. Don't argue with it. Just let it be what it was: a good thing, given. If more come, let them come. The bell holds the time.
Al-mukadhdhibin. Woe that day to the deniers, said ten times in al-Mursalat, often right after a gift: water, body, ground. Today's word.

Your line: don't deny it. This stretch ran from the scattering winds through the balance, which of his favors, a house near you, al-Qalam, constant in prayer and adhkar, to here. Today, when something good arrives, accept it out loud. Day six hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Al-Mursalat is recited in prayer and in personal reading; its refrain returns ten times, and commentators read each return against the sign that comes just before it.
